newsitem.title: UK: MARK SOFTER ON CROSSES AFTER FIXED BUBA REPO.
newsitem.headline: MARK SOFTER ON CROSSES AFTER FIXED BUBA REPO.

text.p: The mark eased against its Eurocrosses on Tuesday after the Bundesbank set its repurchase tender at an unchanged fixed 3.0 percent, signalling unchanged monetary policy.

Currency markets had speculated the Bundesbank might depart from its policy of setting fixed-rate repo tenders at 3.00 percent in order to halt the mark's slide against the dollar and European currencies this year.
Traders, however, said the market remained cautious as speculation regarding a repo move had only been postponed until next week's tender announcement.

"Its a two-week repo, but obviously there is another one next week. And they only announced one, so it means they are watching things very closely - that is why the dollar has not gone up as much as expected," said Lee Ferridge, currency strategist at Commerzbank.

Analysts said while the mark was a touch softer, this suspense will keep the unit from sliding too far. Analysts said speculation of such a move is likely to persist at least until next week, when the central bank will be calling for bids for money-market funds at conditions which have not yet been announced.

At 0735 GMT mark/French franc was trading at 3.3692/97, off lows hit immediately after the announcement, but only a touch down from 3.3695/00 ahead of the news and 3.3696/3.3700 in late Europe on Monday.
Mark/Swiss franc stood at 81.82/86 almost unchanged from 81.84/86 ahead of the news and 82.08/11. Mark/Italian lira was at 974.70/5.00 against 975.40/975.60 in late Europe.
Ferridge said while overall the news was slightly mark negative, the market was somewhat disappointed in that uncertainty over German rates continues to overhang the marketplace.
"The market is a little bit disappointed," said Commerzbank's Ferridge.
But German inflation figures out on Tuesday also added to perceptions that money-market rates are poised to rise.

Inflation rose to 1.9 percent year-on-year in July, its highest rate since June 1995. The month-on-month rise in the consumer price index was 0.5 percent, the highest since January 1997, the Federal Statistics Office said on Tuesday.

"The feeling is that money-markets will be drifting up in Germany...Growth is picking up and inflation is another reason why the market will be looking for a nudge-up in rates," said Michael Lewis, senior international economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
Elsewhere, the French franc was little moved after data showed July consumer prices fell 0.2 percent but rose 1.0 percent year on year.
